section_summary: This section documents the evolution of Japan's foreign exchange and monetary policies from December 1931 through September 1937, beginning with the reimposition of the gold export embargo and subsequent yen depreciation. It details government measures to peg and stabilize exchange rates, the enactment and tightening of the Foreign Exchange Control Law, and the growing economic strains caused by capital investment in Manchukuo. Following the outbreak of the North China incident in 1937, the documents highlight drastic restrictions on non-essential imports, bureaucratic delays that froze approximately 30 million yen of American funds in Japan, and growing fears of an impending general moratorium on foreign exchange obligations.

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note for Despatch No. 406 concerning the effect of lifting the gold embargo on foreign exchange.
subfiles.summary: Document file note recording Despatch No. 406 on foreign exchange and gold embargo lifting.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Despatch No. 406

subfiles.about: Despatch reporting growing sentiment in Japan toward reimposing an embargo on gold specie exports.
subfiles.summary: Counselor Neville reports increasing pressure from financiers, industrialists, and the opposition Seiyukai party to reimpose a gold embargo following heavy specie outflows, Britain's departure from gold, and Manchurian military costs. Finance Minister Inouye defended the free gold policy, arguing trade deficits could be managed through invisible receipts.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 406: Reimposition of Gold Embargo

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note regarding a legal inquiry on the yen-ruble exchange agreement for fisheries disputes.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference note recording an inquiry by Davis, Polk, Wardwell, Gardiner & Reed concerning yen-ruble exchange values.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Inquiry on Russo-Japanese Fisheries Exchange Agreement

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note on rumors that Japan planned to adopt an exchange control system.
subfiles.summary: Note regarding Economic Adviser Feis's memorandum on rumors that Japan is adopting foreign exchange control.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Rumor of Japanese Exchange Control

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note regarding Diet legislation granting the Finance Minister authority to control exchange.
subfiles.summary: Document file note referencing Despatch No. 38 on Japanese exchange control legislation.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Despatch No. 38 on Exchange Control Legislation

subfiles.about: Extract from Despatch No. 38 describing the Diet's passage of a capital flight prevention law.
subfiles.summary: Reports that the Diet passed a bill empowering the Finance Minister to control capital export transactions and require sales of foreign currencies and bonds.
subfiles.title: Excerpt from Despatch No. 38: Exchange Control

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note on the application of the capital flight prevention law to Chosen, Taiwan, and Karafuto.
subfiles.summary: Note on a report from Seoul regarding application of capital flight prevention laws to Japanese external territories.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Capital Flight Law in Dependencies

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note on statements by French High Commissioner de Martel regarding yen depreciation.
subfiles.summary: Note regarding High Commissioner de Martel's statement in Beirut concerning the economic impact of yen depreciation.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Despatch No. 579 on Yen Depreciation

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting Japanese financial reaction to the United States dollar revaluation announcement.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports no changes in Japanese banking or exchange conditions following the U.S. dollar revaluation announcement, noting authorities are adopting a watchful waiting attitude.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 20: Effect of U.S. Dollar Revaluation

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting that higher silver prices have negligible economic impact on Japan.
subfiles.summary: Grew advises that increased silver bullion prices stimulated local silver speculation but have negligible commercial or financial influence due to Japan's minimal silver production and usage.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 32: Silver Prices in Japan

subfiles.about: Official paraphrase of Telegram No. 32 on the economic impact of silver price rises.
subfiles.summary: Paraphrased telegram stating silver price increases prompted local market speculation but hold no significant effect for Japanese trade or industry.
subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Telegram No. 32: Silver Prices in Japan

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note reporting that U.S. dollar devaluation revived debate over devaluing the yen.
subfiles.summary: Note regarding Despatch No. 664 on how dollar devaluation revived discussion of Japanese yen devaluation.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Despatch No. 664 on Dollar Devaluation

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note on a report outlining Japanese financial conditions after the arrest of the former Vice Minister of Finance.
subfiles.summary: Note referencing Commercial Attache Williams's report on financial fallout from the arrest of the former Vice Minister of Finance.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Special Financial Report No. 26

subfiles.about: Memorandum analyzing Tokyo Consulate General's report on Japan's foreign exchange strategy and dollar debentures.
subfiles.summary: Reviews Tokyo's report on Japan's policy of maintaining the yen between 20 and 23 dollars to stimulate exports. Analyzes bank capacity to absorb deficit bonds and notes that dollar-denominated Japanese debentures will be repaid only in paper dollars.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Japanese Foreign Exchange Policy

subfiles.about: Comprehensive consular report tracing Japan's exchange policies, export boom, exchange pegging, and the Exchange Control Act of 1933.
subfiles.summary: Vice Consul Hutchinson details three stages of exchange policy from laissez-faire after the 1931 gold embargo to active pegging between $20 and $23 following the 1933 U.S. banking crisis. Depreciated yen spurred an export boom in textiles, leading authorities to view low exchange as essential despite foreign dumping complaints. The report also examines debt payment in paper dollars and summarizes the March 1933 Foreign Exchange Control Act.
subfiles.title: Voluntary Report: Japanese Government Policy with Regard to Foreign Exchange

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note on Embassy advice that Japan had not altered its foreign exchange policy.
subfiles.summary: Document file note referencing Telegram No. 223 regarding maintenance of Japanese exchange policy.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Telegram No. 223 on Exchange Policy

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting Japanese efforts to peg the yen at one shilling two pence to prevent steep drops.
subfiles.summary: Neville reports the Yokohama Specie Bank aligned its London buying rates to prevent a precipitate fall below one shilling two pence, avoiding foreign accusations of competitive currency depreciation.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 223: Maintenance of Yen-Sterling Rate

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note regarding a suggestion to threaten tariffs on Japanese silk unless gold price increases cease.
subfiles.summary: Note on Committee for the Nation letter suggesting U.S. tariff threats against Japanese silk over gold pricing.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Committee for the Nation Letter on Gold and Silk

subfiles.about: Memorandum answering an inquiry on the relative depreciation, purchasing power, and price indices of the yen.
subfiles.summary: Examines League of Nations data showing yen depreciation of 66 percent from gold parity and 43 percent discounts against the dollar and pound. Compares wholesale prices and cost of living, noting the yen's purchasing power parity.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Depreciation of the Yen

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note on reports concerning a movement to use Japanese yen in Shanghai.
subfiles.summary: Note referencing Despatch No. 102 from Shanghai regarding efforts to promote Japanese yen circulation.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Despatch No. 102 on Japanese Yen in Shanghai

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note discussing potential further inflation of the yen to preserve competitive price advantages.
subfiles.summary: Note regarding Economic Adviser Veatch's memorandum on British press suggestions that Japan might inflate the yen to preserve export competitiveness.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Memorandum on Japanese Foreign Trade and Inflation

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note recording conversation with the Japanese Embassy on the January 1937 exchange regulations.
subfiles.summary: Note regarding Dooman's conversation with Japanese Embassy officials seeking clarification of Treasury statements on newly implemented exchange controls.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Memorandum on Exchange Control Operation

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note on Diet statements denying plans to devalue the yen and defending gold exports.
subfiles.summary: Note referencing Commercial Attache Williams's report on official denials of yen devaluation and justification of gold shipments.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Special Report No. 155 on Yen Devaluation

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note reporting weak exchange markets and Japanese refusal to join the Tripartite Stabilization Agreement.
subfiles.summary: Note referencing Williams's report that Japan saw no need to join the US-British-French Tripartite Stabilization Agreement.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Special Report No. 158 on Tripartite Agreement

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note on the extension and amendment of foreign exchange control regulations.
subfiles.summary: Note referencing Tower's report on Department of Finance ordinances amending and tightening 1933 exchange control regulations.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Report No. 183 on Foreign Exchange Regulations

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting anticipated tightening of the import licensing threshold from 30,000 to 1,000 yen.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports expected lowering of the permit-free import exchange limit from 30,000 to 1,000 yen to curb evasion by straw men, amidst an adverse trade balance exceeding 500 million yen and mounting gold exports.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 138: Revision of Import Exchange Licensing

subfiles.about: Official paraphrase of Telegram No. 138 regarding import exchange license revisions.
subfiles.summary: Paraphrased text outlining impending reductions in permit exemptions to 1,000 yen, restrictions on non-essential remittances, and concern over trade deficits and gold depletion.
subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Telegram No. 138: Revision of Import Exchange Licensing

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note quoting Tokyo Telegram No. 138 transmitted to Butterworth.
subfiles.summary: Note recording transmission of Tokyo's telegram on import licensing revisions to Treasury representative Butterworth.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Treasury Letter on Tokyo Telegram

subfiles.about: Memorandum commenting on economic controls and internal divisions within the Japanese Government.
subfiles.summary: Internal note predicting import controls and moderated Manchukuo investments will occur without decisive resolution of internal governmental divisions.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Division in Japanese Government

subfiles.about: Memorandum identifying heavy capital investment in Manchukuo as the primary cause of Japan's exchange drain.
subfiles.summary: Feis analyzes an Institute of Pacific Relations study showing Manchukuo investments cause Japan's exchange crisis, framing policy choices around an internal struggle between military control advocates and moderates.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Drain of Japanese Exchange by Manchukuo Investments

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note inquiring whether to lodge an informal protest against tightened exchange restrictions.
subfiles.summary: Note regarding State Department telegram inquiring on the advisability of protesting stricter Japanese exchange restrictions.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Telegram No. 105 on Proposed Exchange Protest

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note on the promulgation reducing exchange exemptions to 1,000 yen per month.
subfiles.summary: Document file note referencing Telegram No. 182 reporting the reduction of monthly exchange permit exemptions to 1,000 yen.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Telegram No. 182 on Promulgation of Exchange Regulations

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting promulgation of revised exchange rules reducing permit-free transactions to 1,000 yen.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports revised regulations cutting the monthly permit-free allowance from 30,000 to 1,000 yen, exempting prior contracts and existing cargo shipments.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 182: Promulgation of Revised Exchange Regulations

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note recommending an expression of concern over exchange controls restricting American goods.
subfiles.summary: Note referencing Telegram No. 184 suggesting U.S. concern be expressed over exchange controls favoring rearmament over American imports.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Telegram No. 184 on Import Priorities and U.S. Concern

subfiles.about: Telegram detailing government-banker conferences following troop deployments to North China and resulting financial strains.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports government consultations with bankers seeking support during the North China incident. Details war risk insurance mandates, stock exchange declines, and banking fears of frozen forward exchange commitments.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 194: Financial Impact of North China Incident

subfiles.about: Official paraphrase of Telegram No. 194 on financial measures following North China hostilities.
subfiles.summary: Paraphrased telegram covering Hirota's appeal to financiers, metropolitan bank pledges to sustain the exchange rate, Tokyo stock market drops, and banking anxieties over frozen remittances.
subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Telegram No. 194: Financial Impact of North China Incident

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note on Japanese administrative delays in issuing exchange permits, citing California Packing Corporation.
subfiles.summary: Note referencing Despatch No. 2476 describing procrastination in granting exchange permits and the California Packing Corporation case.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Despatch No. 2476 on Exchange Control Practices

subfiles.about: Despatch detailing bureaucratic confusion, administrative delays, and priority rules in the enforcement of exchange controls.
subfiles.summary: Grew describes widespread confusion and bureaucratic paralysis in Japan's Foreign Exchange Control Division, which lacked adequate staff. Priority is granted to munitions, national defense plant expansion, and export raw materials, while commercial applications—such as California Packing Corporation's canned goods and a major scrap iron purchase—suffer indefinite delays without formal rejection.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2476: Operation of Japanese Foreign Exchange Control

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting 30 million yen of American funds frozen in Japan and imminent suspension of foreign exchange payments.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports that 30 million yen in proceeds from American consignment sales are blocked by administrative permit delays. With virtually no commercial exchange permits issued, planned import quotas prioritizing munitions, and heavy gold drains, observers anticipate a complete suspension of foreign payments before December.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 258: Frozen American Funds and Commercial Exchange Suspension

subfiles.about: Transmittal slip forwarding a partial paraphrase of Tokyo Telegram No. 258 on Japanese exchange.
subfiles.summary: Secretary of State transmits a paraphrase of Tokyo Telegram No. 258 on Japanese exchange to the Treasury.
subfiles.title: State Department Transmittal Note on Telegram No. 258

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note on Diet legislation controlling domestic industry to support exchange restrictions.
subfiles.summary: Note referencing Despatch No. 2529 regarding a bill submitted to the Diet to control domestic industry.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Despatch No. 2529 on Industry Control Legislation

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note advising cotton shippers of strict Japanese exchange limitations on cotton imports.
subfiles.summary: Note referencing Osaka telegram warning cotton shippers that exchange restrictions require confirmed credits.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Telegram on Osaka Cotton Exchange Restrictions

subfiles.about: Telegram advising warning American cotton exporters that exchange for cotton imports is strictly restricted.
subfiles.summary: Consul Krentz warns that Japanese exchange control may freeze up to two-thirds of the value of cotton in transit and advises shippers to require confirmed credits.
subfiles.title: Telegram: Exchange Control on Cotton Imports

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note reporting the closure of the Osaka Cotton Exchange for alleged profiteering.
subfiles.summary: Note referencing Commercial Attache Williams's report on the government closure of the Osaka Cotton Exchange for profiteering.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Weekly Report No. 9 on Osaka Cotton Exchange Closure

subfiles.about: Cover despatch transmitting Commercial Attache Williams's memorandum on frozen American funds in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew transmits Commercial Attache Williams's memorandum on frozen American funds without comment due to pouch departure.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2535: Transmittal of Memorandum on American Funds in Japan

subfiles.about: Commercial Attache memorandum detailing 30 million yen of frozen American funds and impending Japanese debt moratoria.
subfiles.summary: Williams details how Japanese authorities withhold exchange permits for 30 million yen owed to American consignors, while forcing Japanese firms to repatriate 150 million yen in foreign earnings. He warns that soaring military expenditures from the North China conflict, unmarketable domestic bonds, and a projected international payments deficit of 300 to 400 million yen make a general foreign debt moratorium likely by December.
subfiles.title: Memorandum: American Funds Frozen in Japan
